item.title: I removed 90% of my VS Code extensions and my workflow didn't break
item.itunes:title: I removed 90% of my VS Code extensions and my workflow didn't break
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I used to treat the VS Code Marketplace like an endless toolbox. Whenever I wanted a new shortcut, visual tweak, or small improvement, I would search for an extension and install it. Over time, that left me with a setup packed with tools I barely remembered adding. I recently decided to take a different approach and see what happened if I removed most of them. Instead of trying to build the perfect extension collection, I wanted to see how far VS Code could take me on its own. The result was more interesting than I expected, and it made me question how much customization I actually needed.

VS Code already handles more coding basics than I realized

Built-in tools handled my daily coding

Once I started using VS Code with my extensions turned off, I was surprised by how much of my everyday coding workflow still worked normally. I could open a project, jump between files, and get the editor to understand what I was working with without adding another layer of customization.

The first thing I noticed was how capable the editor is at understanding code structure. I could jump to a definition, find references, rename symbols, and move around a project without reaching for an extension. Autocomplete and suggestions were also good enough for the languages I use regularly, especially for the basic tasks I perform throughout the day.

Even small things I had previously associated with extensions were already available through VS Code's built-in commands. The Command Palette made it easy to find these features instead of remembering where everything lived.

I had simply stopped checking what VS Code could already do. I had gotten used to installing an extension whenever I wanted a small improvement, without first asking whether the editor already had a solution.

Great built-in formatting and code cleanup support

Less code clutter

The next surprise was how much less I needed to keep my code clean and readable. I had a few extensions installed mainly for quick formatting or small cleanup actions, so I disabled them and started testing what VS Code could handle on its own.

The built-in formatting commands covered the basics I actually used. I could format an entire file or just a selected section without adding another extension for the job. I also found that settings such as format on save made this even more convenient. Once configured, I didn't have to think about formatting every time I made changes.

The same was true for several small cleanup tasks. VS Code could surface quick fixes and code actions when the language support provided them. I could accept a suggested change instead of manually fixing every little issue.

I rebuilt my VS Code setup from scratch this year, and it's the fastest it's ever been

My VS Code was drowning in extensions

By  Ayush Pande

Git, debugging, and terminals were already sitting inside VS Code

Fewer reasons to switch apps

The biggest realization came when I looked at the tools I used around my code every day. I had extensions installed for parts of my workflow that I assumed needed extra help, but VS Code already had much of it covered.

Git was a good example. I could see changed files, review diffs, stage changes, create commits, switch branches, and deal with basic merge conflicts directly from the Source Control view. I didn't need another interface just to handle the Git tasks I regularly performed.

Debugging was another area where I had underestimated the editor. I could set breakpoints, step through my code, inspect variables, and use the debug console without installing a separate debugging experience. Once I had the right language support available, the workflow felt surprisingly complete.

Then there was the integrated terminal. I could run scripts, install packages, start development servers, and use Git commands without opening another application. I often kept terminal-related extensions around for convenience, but I found myself using the built-in terminal almost exclusively.

I still did not go completely extension-free

My stripped-down VS Code setup feels better to use

After stripping things back, I didn't decide that every extension had to go. That would have missed the point of the exercise. Some extensions genuinely add capabilities that aren't covered by VS Code itself, and those are the ones I was happy to keep.

Language-specific tools were the first group I left alone. Some languages and frameworks need dedicated support for features that go beyond basic editing. I also kept extensions that fit how I work on particular projects, rather than removing them just to make the extension count look impressive.

I also found that some extensions were worth keeping because they solved a problem in a way I preferred. An extension doesn't have to be essential to be useful. If I use a feature regularly and it saves me time, I don't see a reason to remove it just for the sake of having a smaller setup.

I've only kept these 6 VS Code extensions after deep-cleaning the code editor

I can't use VS Code without these handy extensions

5
By  Ayush Pande

A leaner VS Code was all I needed

Stripping VS Code back changed how I think about extensions. I no longer see a long list of installed tools as a sign of a better setup. I care more about whether each one earns its place. My editor now feels less crowded and easier to maintain, while still doing everything I need. Sometimes, the best upgrade is simply removing what you stopped needing.

item.title: After trying countless Jellyfin apps, I finally found my all-in-one favorite
item.itunes:title: After trying countless Jellyfin apps, I finally found my all-in-one favorite
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I've used virtually every Jellyfin client app currently available. Of course, new ones keep popping up every day. One of the awesome things about the Jellyfin community is that there's always something new to try. While some alternative apps focus on a single media type or platform, like Findroid for video or Jellybox for music, Pelagica delivers all of my media in a lightweight UI.

It includes light and dark themes, a video player, and a music player with the controls you'd expect from a media app. You don't need to install separate apps for different media types. It also works on multiple devices, including Windows, Mac, Linux, Samsung smart TVs running Tizen, and LG TVs on WebOS. You can also install a web version via the Docker image.

Pelagica is responsive

A lightweight Jellyfin client

Some of the Jellyfin clients I have tried are slow and hog a lot of resources. Pelagica is fast and responsive, with load times that are far quicker than other clients I've tried. It doesn't hog system resources on my PC or Mac either. It runs smoothly and starts playing videos more quickly than others, including the official Jellyfin client or Moonfin. It integrates with different services, like Seerr to discover new movies, Streamystats for recommendations on the home page, and Kefintweak Watchlist to manage watchlists,

It is also faster and easier to navigate than the standard Jellyfin Web app (or client) I use for verifying videos work after adding new content to my server or restructuring my media library. The app is light and offers a zippy interface that lets me move quickly between videos and other libraries. A responsive UI makes playing my content easier.

In addition to being a responsive front end for the Jellyfin client, it supports multiple languages, including German, Spanish, Japanese, and others. If you are unsure whether you want to try another Jellyfin app, the developer set it up so you can test it out on the Pelagica live web demo. There isn't a mobile or streaming device version yet, but you can use it on desktop, smart TVs, or the web. Whatever device you have, you can find the latest release on the Pelagica GitHub page.

It also has a host of settings you can tweak to improve the app's experience. Go to the Pelagica Config section to add your Seerr and Streamystats URLs to improve recommendations on the home screen and via search. You can also adjust watched badges, manage sections on the home screen, add links to other sites or web apps, change themes, and a lot more.

I finally found the Android Jellyfin app I've always wanted

I've tried several Jellyfin apps but this one hits all the marks.

By  Brian Burgess

Pelagica for Jellyfin does it all

An all-in-one app

I have run Pelagica on Windows and Mac, and it runs well on both systems. Unfortunately, I don't have a smart TV with Tizen or WebOS to try it. But from the minute I launched the app, I was impressed by how fast and responsive it is. I can fly through my media library faster than other clients that can sometimes get bogged down.

Pelagica is a Jellyfin client for the web, desktop, and select smart TV brands. For movies and shows, it breaks down and displays the IMDB information that you see on some other clients. It shows backdrops, poster art, and banners included in your library. That isn't something unique to Pelagica, but it's nice to know it's there, it works, and it's fast.

It is minimalistic in how it shows media; it doesn't show poster art, thumbnails, or banners for everything while I'm searching through my media library. I was taken aback at first, but I found that is one reason it is so snappy. Plus, it really doesn't have to. The title descriptions are always present. I still have a top row that displays my titles, which I can click to see the full description.

Jellyfin
iOS compatible
Yes
Android compatible
Yes
See at Jellyfin Jellyfin 12 (RC5)

Finding content on Pelagica

Straightforward search and browsing

It lets me search through my entire library and brings up the results fast. It also arranges my titles into categories like Sci-fi, Western, Dramas, Thrillers, etc. I can click through those categories to find what I want to watch or search directly for a specific title.

Once I click the play button, the movie, show, or music loads instantaneously. It doesn't include many extra playback controls, but it gives me the basics you would expect from a media player. However, when you download the Windows .exe file, it will flag it as malware. Just allow it through anyway; it's trusted and safe. I've been running it on multiple machines for a week.

Pelagica launches quickly, uses few system resources, loads content faster than other clients, and makes it easy to find my media. In addition to browsing through media categories, I can use the top toolbar to choose what I want to watch in my library. Or, I can select the home page for content I want to continue to watch or something recently added. Another cool thing it does is break down my movies and shows by the studio that produced them.

6 lessons I learned after ditching Plex for Jellyfin on my NAS

A self-hosted setup that finally feels mine

20
By  Karandeep Singh

The all-in-one Jellyfin client

I have used the word fast a lot in this article, and I'm not sorry. On top of its capabilities, Pelagica's speed is the most impressive feature it has. What I am sorry about is that it isn't available on more devices — namely streaming sticks and boxes. However, I say that about many of the cool Jellyfin apps and plugins I've covered. Still, if you want speed and functionality, Pelagica delivers.

item.title: I stopped emailing files to myself, and now a tiny open-source app moves them between my devices instead
item.itunes:title: I stopped emailing files to myself, and now a tiny open-source app moves them between my devices instead
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
For years, my inbox doubled as a temporary storage space. If I had a file on my iPhone that I needed on my Windows PC, I would simply email it to myself. It worked, but it was hardly an elegant solution.

The funny thing is, I never really stopped to question why I was doing it. Email was just there, so I used it. Then I came across LocalSend, a tiny app built around transferring files between nearby devices. It made me rethink a habit I had barely noticed. Once I started using it, sending files between my devices became a much less annoying part of my day.

item.title: I ditched motion sensors for mmWave radar, and my lights never plunge into darkness anymore
item.itunes:title: I ditched motion sensors for mmWave radar, and my lights never plunge into darkness anymore
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
For so many smart home builders, the reality is you're sat at your desk or on the sofa reading an article or watching a movie, and suddenly the room plunges into pitch-black darkness. You're forced to vigorously wave your arms around just to trick a wall sensor into turning the lights back on.

Traditional motion sensors fail because passive infrared sensors don't actually detect presence; they detect radiant heat in motion. The moment you sit still, the delta in infrared radiation drops to zero. To the PIR sensor, the room is completely empty. There are workarounds, but these are messy, like bumping timeout intervals to 20 or 30 minutes, which can waste energy, or adding multiple PIR sensors at odd angles.

True occupancy automation requires replacing binary motion triggers with an interlocking presence engine by combining mmWave micro radar, sub-meter Bluetooth, and RSSI beacons and hardware state telemetry inside Home Assistant. You can build a zero-latency, unbreakable presence tracking matrix that never plunges you into darkness again.

This cool ESP32‑S3 project is like a Geiger counter but for finding your phone instead of radiation

You'll actually want to follow the clicks this time.

1
By  Simon Batt

Traditional presence sensors suck

The technology feels outdated

The physics and silicone differences between legacy infrared detection and modern active sensing are the reason why PIR failed and the reason why mmWave radars replaced it.

PIR, or pyroelectric sensors, rely on a Fresnel lens splitting a field of view into zones. It requires an object with a surface temperature different from the ambient room temperature to physically cross from one optoelectronic zone to another. If you don't cross the field of view, you're technically invisible.

With mmWave sensors, they operate at 24GHz or 60GHz, and the sensor broadcasts high-frequency electromagnetic waves and measures the Doppler phase shift of returning reflections. It detects micro-movements down to fractions of a millimeter, including the physical rise and fall of your chest while breathing or the pulse at your wrist. This means that even if you're not actually moving, the natural movement that your body makes ensures that the sensor detects that you're there.

Alongside this, a lot of modern multi-target radar sensors don't just output a binary occupied (yes/no) feed. They instead stream real-time coordinates, allowing Home Assistant to draw virtual zones around a couch, bed, or desk for even further automation.

You don't just have to opt for mmWave

There are so many ways to detect presence

No-motion presence engines have a range of uses and can be used in many ways. While they continue to track you without you needing any traditional motion sensors, the first is obviously continuous micro presence via the mmWave radar, which sets the baseline. You can place these sensors strategically in living areas, offices, and bedrooms, and they'll capture static motionless occupancy even when you're reading, working, or sleeping, with zero timeout delays.

You can combine this with identity and microlocalization via BLE beaming. mmWave doesn't know who is in the room even though it can tell a human is there. The fix is to deploy a $4 ESP32 node running ESP Presence or use Home Assistant's Bermuda BLE triangulation. It can then track the Bluetooth Low Energy advertisement signals from a smartwatch or your phone. That way, the house can calculate signal distance by measured RSSI values and determine who's in the room. As a result, the office doesn't just illuminate; it actually loads your specific lighting preferences and desk type presets because it detects your watch within a 1 m radius.

An issue you might encounter is that if you sleep under a thick down duvet, even 60 GHz mmWave radar can occasionally miss shallow breathing if it's obstructed, or ceiling fans can cause phantom false positives. The fix here can be inexpensive automotive weight sensor mats or DIY load cells tucked beneath the mattress or desk chair cushion. Then you can ensure that sitting down or lying in your bed asserts a definitive physical binary state that overrides all optical and radar logic.

Inferred state telemetry is a great way to track presence in a room as well, so that you can be 100% certain that where you are in the house is tracked regardless of any of your sensors. You can do this by using `hass.agent` on your desktop, which monitors active user input (like mouse or keyboard use) or even just an active session state. Or you can use smart plug power monitoring on your TV or gaming PC. That way, if either of these is drawing a certain amount of wattage, the living room occupancy state is pinned to occupied, regardless of whether anyone is moving in front of a sensor.

So what hardware do you need?

Everything is cost-effective

What hardware should you be purchasing in order to deploy these automations?

The main thing worth investing in is the radar itself. You can pick up a cheap radar module for less than $10 on AliExpress and pair it with an ESP32 or a pre-packaged commercial unit like the Aqara FP2 or Apollo Automation MS-2. In total, these are extremely cost-effective and allow you to ensure you have constant presence detection.

Invest in a room beacon. Flash existing spare ESP32 boards with ESP Presence and drop one in each key room to ingest smartwatch BLE advertisements.

If you do want to take advantage of the chair/bed hack, then buying a $6 12 V automotive seat occupancy sensor and connecting it to the GPIO pin of an existing USB home node (with an internal pull-up resistor) before sliding it under the cushion of your desk chair will ensure that any time you're sat down, a sensor can pick up on it and therefore knows that the room is occupied.

Make your smart home work for you

Don't sit in darkness

A smart home shouldn't force you to change your physical behavior. The moment an automation demands that you wave your hands, shout at a voice system, or open a phone app, the technology has essentially failed. Instead of using cheap plastic PIR motion sensors that keep leaving you in the dark and require you to wave your hands around like you're a circus, you can build a multi-layered presence engine with radar, contact telemetry, and local radio beacons that make your smart home behave like it actually knows you're there.

item.title: My home server runs on a 10-year-old PC, and it still does everything I need
item.itunes:title: My home server runs on a 10-year-old PC, and it still does everything I need
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
My home server is the heartbeat of my home office. It acts as my photo and video library backup point, my NAS, my local AI node, and media library, all while being built from parts I already had. This system was collecting dust for many months in my closet, and had sat without a CPU cooler and boot drive until I revived it about a decade after it was initially built. The Skylake-era i7 and Z170 board provide more than enough headroom alone for a decent home server for self-hosting, but I've since built upon it with incremental upgrades that have made it more reliable and capable than anything I'd be able to buy off of a retail shelf right now.

6 reasons why you might want to pick SBCs and mini-PCs over server-grade hardware

Hardcore server rigs may appeal more to home lab lovers, but there are just as many perks with consumer-rated systems

2
By  Ayush Pande

The workloads that matter to me are I/O bound

Most of a home server's workload isn't CPU bound

You really don't need much raw CPU horsepower for a conventional home server, even if you plan on running more than just a couple of services. The i7-6700K in this system has aged unusually well for applications like this.

My Samba share, for instance, tops out somewhere around 250 MB/s in practice on my 2.5GbE NIC, which really isn't a substantial load for this chip. ZFS on a two-drive mirror like I run is super undemanding even at the worst of times. The pool spends its time waiting on the disks more than it does the processor. And because I run most things in LXCs rather than VMs, they share the host kernel directly instead of stacking a guest OS and its accompanying overhead on top of every single workload. Now, if I were to run a dozen VMs, a Kubernetes cluster, or run crazy compression at scale, this i7 would be a serious bottleneck.

I used an Intel N100 mini-PC as a standalone Proxmox node – it went really well

Besides being able to self-host multiple containers, it can even run a few VMs

2
By  Ayush Pande

The GPU handles what the CPU can't

item.title: After years with Niagara Launcher, this open-source alternative finally won me over
item.itunes:title: After years with Niagara Launcher, this open-source alternative finally won me over
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I've tried plenty of Android launchers over the years, but I rarely found a reason to change the one I was already using. Niagara Launcher had become my default, so switching to something unfamiliar wasn't high on my list. Then I came across Escape Launcher, an open-source project that takes a noticeably different approach to the Android home screen. I installed it mostly out of curiosity, expecting to test it briefly and move on. Instead, I kept coming back to it. The experience made me look differently at what I actually want from a launcher, and whether a simpler approach can work better for me.

I prefer Niagara launcher for years

Niagara was hard to replace

For years, I relied on Niagara Launcher for my Pixel device. Once I got used to its layout, going back to a traditional Android home screen felt unnecessarily busy. I liked having my most-used apps within easy reach instead of spreading icons across multiple pages.

What worked for me was how little maintenance it needed. I didn't have to keep rearranging icons or deciding which apps belonged on which screen. My phone felt organized without requiring much effort from me. Even when I installed new apps, I rarely felt the need to change how everything was set up.

It kept things focused on the apps I actually opened. After using it for so long, the interface became second nature. I knew where everything was, and that familiarity made it difficult to imagine replacing it with another launcher. At that point, Niagara was simply the way I used my Android phone.

I replaced the Pixel Launcher over one limitation I couldn't ignore

The Pixel Launcher improved, but customization still fell disappointingly short.

6
By  Yash Patel

Escape launcher made me rethink

This minimalist launcher caught me off guard

Escape Launcher caught my attention because it approached the home screen from a completely different angle. Instead of giving me another collection of icons, widgets, and customization options to manage, it felt almost like a blank space. The initial time was strange because I was so used to Niagara's familiar layout.

What stood out to me was the simplicity of the interface. Escape Launcher doesn't try to fill the screen with information or make the phone look impressive. It feels deliberately plain, and I found that surprisingly refreshing. There was something appealing about opening my phone and seeing so little competing for my attention.

Escape Launcher is open source and available through F-Droid. That made it easy for me to try without committing to another closed launcher ecosystem.

The more I looked at it, the more I realized I had been thinking about launchers in terms of what they could add to my phone. Escape Launcher made me consider the opposite: what if a launcher worked better by getting out of my way? That question was enough to make me keep using it.

It changed my daily phone habits

Less friction in my daily routine

After using Escape Launcher for a while, I noticed that its features were changing how I interacted with my phone. The simple text-based interface meant I wasn't constantly looking at a grid of colorful icons. I could search for an app, open it, and move on without much fuss.

I also liked having quick access to apps and other parts of my phone without filling the home screen with shortcuts. The launcher keeps the interface focused, so I didn't feel the need to arrange everything around me. Even basic things like finding an app or returning to the home screen felt more deliberate.

Another feature I appreciated was the ability to customize what appears in the launcher without turning it into a complicated setup process. I could keep the experience suited to how I actually use my phone instead of spending time tweaking every small detail.

It is not better at everything

It's great, but not for everyone

As much as I like Escape Launcher, I wouldn't say it is a better launcher for everyone. Its approach is quite specific, and that can be a drawback if you want your Android home screen to do more.

I can see some users missing the visual flexibility of a conventional launcher. If you enjoy setting up widgets, arranging icons, using custom layouts, or changing the look of your home screen regularly, Escape Launcher may feel too restrictive. It isn't really designed for people who treat their home screen as a space for personalization.

There is a small adjustment period, and the stripped-back design can feel unusual if you're coming from a more traditional launcher. For me, those limitations don't outweigh what I like about it. But that's the important point: Escape Launcher works because its minimal approach fits how I want to use my phone. For someone with different priorities, another launcher could easily be the better choice.

4 launchers that turn my boring Pixel home screen into something actually useful

Give your Pixel a fresh look with these powerful launchers.

4
By  Yash Patel

Sometimes, the best launcher is the one you forget

I didn't expect to replace Niagara Launcher after using it for so long, but Escape Launcher changed my perspective. It isn't trying to be the most feature-packed option, and that's exactly what makes it interesting. After giving it a proper chance, I found myself choosing it without thinking about the switch anymore. For my Android setup, that says more than any feature list ever could.

I recently acquired a Bambu Labs A2L to design parts for all my hobby projects as well as home improvement tools. Looking at the sheer breadth of options and designs over on websites like MakerWorld and Thingiverse has also helped me discover solutions to problems I didn't even know I had. Part of that is a series of kitchen fixes that solve everyday practical problems. Some are things I could probably purchase; others not,

It's the definition of what makes 3D printing so exciting. I can find or make simple designs that solve a specific problem anytime I need it. I've spent time printing out these fixes for my kitchen, and they've all addressed everyday issues and made my life easier. They might do the same for you.

7 practical problems I solved with a 3D printer

My 3D printer has proven itself not just fun, but also a household problem-solver. Here's how

2
By  Jeff Butts

Sink saver

A simple two-level design keeps rinsing water and residue away

The sink saver is perhaps my favorite 3D print simply because it solves a problem I hadn't even thought about until I came across the model over at MakerWorld. Anytime I rinse a bowl or a cup, I have to hold it up at an angle to not clog up the drain. It's a problem I'm sure most of us face. Nor do I want to just put it down in the sink, which might have not-so-clean water.

So, I printed a sink saver. It's an ingenious two-level contraption printed in, well, two parts. There's an upper section in which I can rinse and empty out water. This part holds any residue that drops alongside. It also has slots in it to let water through. Once I'm done rinsing the utensils, the remaining water drains away rather than sitting around at the bottom.

It adds a single step to my routine but automatically saves me the hassle of dealing with a clogged drain. Very handy.

item.title: My old Fire TV Stick spends all day as a photo frame now, and it cost me nothing to set up
item.itunes:title: My old Fire TV Stick spends all day as a photo frame now, and it cost me nothing to set up
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Before you toss your old Fire TV Stick because it's too old and slow, look for ways to repurpose it. One thing you can do is use it to turn your TV into a digital photo frame. As a Prime member, you get unlimited photo storage at no extra cost.

It's an overlooked feature that gives an old Fire TV Stick a useful purpose. I uploaded my pictures to Amazon and now have an endlessly rotating carousel of images on the big screen.

Creating a Fire TV Stick photo frame

An old stick and HDMI port

Reusing your out-of-date and sluggish Fire TV as a photo frame is a common repurposing scenario. You don't need to buy anything since you already bought the stick years ago. You don't need a new TV, just an extra HDMI port on the one in your living room or on a spare TV in another room.

Free photo storage is included with an Amazon Prime account, which most people consider an essential annual bill anyway. Plug the old stick into a TV you want to display pictures on, upload pictures to Amazon Photos, and let the stick run the back end of your photo frame experience.

Downloading the Photos app to my phone made it much easier to add photos to collections to display in a photo frame. I can choose to have it back up all my photos or just the ones I want displayed on the big screen. I can also choose the photos that display later by adding them.

Setting up the photo frame

Some housekeeping

While the process is as basic as plugging in a stick, there are a few things to cover. The Fire TV Stick still needs the ability to connect to Wi-Fi and have a working power adapter. The Amazon Photos app needs to be installed on the stick, and photos need to be uploaded. I also recommend doing some light photo organization by sorting pictures into albums and favorites; otherwise, the entire library will display randomly.

Choosing how the Fire TV Stick displays photos and tweaking settings is easy enough through the Photos app and screensaver or Ambient (depending on the stick's age) screen settings. You can tweak photo behavior through the Fire TV Stick's menu to choose transitions and shuffling, and quickly adjust other photo display settings.

Amazon Photos
Starts at $2/month

Adjusting the Fire TV Stick photo frame

Settings changes on the fly

Getting the photos to look the way you like takes some fiddling with the stick's settings. The settings used will depend on the device. Older sticks have a Screensaver setting, which is a basic slideshow. Newer sticks have an Ambient Experience option. The latter layers photos with widgets, music, and more.

For screensavers, I adjust the idle time before photos display, the slide transitions, and how quickly new photos appear. Ambient settings allow me to add optional weather or calendar widgets and include additional effects. On either device, the Fire TV home screen mess stays out of the way, and only the photos are displayed.

Another thing to keep in mind is that the Fire TV Stick determines how the photos display on the screen and how long they stay up, based on the settings you choose. However, a stick usually won't override the TV set's power timers. So, to use it as an always-on frame, adjust the TV's power settings accordingly.

That old Fire TV Stick still works as a frame

Photo slideshows aren't demanding

Even some of the oldest Fire TV Sticks can be used as a photo frame. A picture slideshow doesn't demand many system resources and is easier to display than 4K video. It isn't as processor-intensive as gaming or heavy multitasking. For example, I used a third-generation (2017 diamond-shaped dongle) Fire TV to create a photo frame, and it worked well as a slideshow with my photos from Amazon Photos.

It had slower transitions between photos, and slide-style effects weren't as responsive as the new sticks I tried, but it did the job well. If someone comes over to the house, they don't know it's an ancient Fire TV running the photo frame in the background. They just like to admire the photos I display. I just don't have the extras of the Ambient Experience to jazz up the photo presentation.

Free to set up, not to maintain

Other cost considerations

While setting up a Fire TV Stick as a photo frame is free, there are costs to consider once it's up and running. Your electricity bill is the most obvious one. To view the photos, the screen must be powered on, which consumes more power than a small e-ink photo frame. You can set it to put the display to sleep after a period, but depending on your HDMI-CEC setup, other devices could interfere.

The Fire TV Stick will also need to stay powered on, which doesn't require much electricity, but is still more than something that wouldn't be used at all. Your Prime Membership will need to be actively maintained — something most forget about anyway. Also, consider what your time is worth and how much effort you want to put into managing your photo library.

4 settings I changed right away on my new Fire TV Stick 4K Max

Amazon's relatively cheap streaming stick has several settings turned on by default that can be frustrating.

6
By  Patrick O'Rourke

Getting more from a Fire TV Stick

Turning my old Fire TV Stick into a photo frame was straightforward using the Amazon Photos app. It provides unlimited photo storage, so it costs nothing to turn my old stick and TV into a digital photo frame.

I can load as many photos as I want and let them run in the background all day, or set a sleep timer on my TV to conserve energy while I'm away. It's simple to get going, and, like other photos, it becomes a talking point when people come over.

item.title: How full your SSD is does more damage to it than anything you actually write
item.itunes:title: How full your SSD is does more damage to it than anything you actually write
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Storage was a luxury back in the day when I bought my first laptop. Slowly, the storage became cheaper, smaller, and faster than a traditional HDD. Before the whole AI crisis that shot up the cost of storage and memory, NVMe SSDs were only slightly more expensive than SATA SSDs, despite a huge difference in read-write speed, primarily due to their connection interface. I have a couple of SSDs that I use and external drives with a SATA enclosure. My main system, a Windows 11 PC, uses a Samsung NVMe SSD.

The first read and write speed check I did in 2021, when the SSD barely had any files except the OS, is different from the speed that I get now. I have filled my drive to about 80 percent, and surprisingly, that's one of the main reasons that the performance has slightly deteriorated. Let's discuss why a lean drive is better than a filled one.

SSD storage gets filled fast

Increasing size of apps, games, and files

When you buy a new laptop or computer, as I did, which has more storage capacity than the previous one, the hesitation to use it judiciously disappears. You start downloading software, test apps and games, and slowly fill up the drive to the brim. I installed several gamesand programs, deployed multiple virtual machines, and left only about 50–100GB of space to move files around. Gradually, the storage performance deteriorated, resulting in somewhat slower write speeds.

5 SSD myths that are simply untrue

Don't fall for these common SSD misunderstandings.

13
By  Jacob Roach

I never performed any cleanup, left virtual machines unattended for weeks, and had game installations that I only played a couple of times. So, I kept a lot of barely important stuff on the main SSD, and it cost me performance and reduced its lifespan. But does an SSD's occupied storage have any relationship with performance or lifespan? Surprisingly, yes, and I learned it a little late.

SSDs don't have moving parts

But more occupancy deteriorates performance

While an SSD can claim more endurance due to its design and the lack of moving parts, it's not susceptible to wear and tear. It uses NAND cells, and each cell uses pages and blocks to write data on them. A page is the smallest unit on an SSD, and a block can have multiple pages. Imagine a fresh drive, and the OS commands the SSD controller (which actually is the brain of the whole thing) to write three pages. It changes the state of these pages, and happily maintains a mapping of where data is stored.

If you boot Proxmox from an SSD, disable these two services to prevent wearing out your drive

A couple of optimizations to help your Proxmox SSD stay in tip-top shape

19
By  Ayush Pande

As the write operations grow, the SSD has to manage the available storage space. It can write/rewrite an empty page, but it can only erase blocks and not pages. There’s nothing you can do about it because it's a design choice of flash storage. Since erase actions can only happen at a block level, if you want to modify something that’s stored at a page level, the mechanism becomes a tad complex. Firstly, the SSD controller decides the viable block and page location to put that data. That specific block might have some valid pages and some with old data.

It cannot simply erase any page; it marks the old pages as “invalid” and writes the new data to unused ones (which can be in the same or other blocks). It then updates the mapping table to point to the new physical location. On a small scale, this looks viable, but problems arise when you have millions of invalid pages.

Fixing invalid pages

Internal SSD processes take a toll

SSD uses garbage collection, a method to reclaim the entire block and make it usable again. To do so, it needs to move the data to another block (or blocks) that have a usable page. item.title: Windows 11 isn't the unstable one — the drivers your PC has been carrying since Windows 10 are
item.itunes:title: Windows 11 isn't the unstable one — the drivers your PC has been carrying since Windows 10 are
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I've been using Windows 11 for almost four years now. I've never liked it, mainly because of the interface and some changes Microsoft madewhen upgrading from Windows 10. But all the hate aside, I'm not going to call Windows 11 an unstable operating system. I think it's quite stable.

And I don't think all the complaints about crashes and BSODs are necessarily the result of an unstable OS. Statistically, over 95% of Windows system crashes and Blue Screens of Death are caused by third-party drivers and hardware conflicts. Many of us have been carrying over drivers from the Windows 10 era, so it's only natural that some of them will result in crashes.

Legacy drivers break Windows 11 more than Windows 11 itself

Those sneaky Windows 10 drivers cause all the trouble

When you upgrade an existing PC from Windows 10 to Windows 11, you often carry over years of outdated drivers. Windows 10 took a decade to build a reliable driver ecosystem. Windows 11 introduced newer hardware requirements, security features, and changes to the underlying software environment. However, older drivers carried over from Windows 10 don’t always interact properly with these newer components, which leads to freezes or sudden crashes.

Plus, many hardware drivers run in kernel mode with deep access to the operating system. That’s necessary for components such as graphics cards, storage controllers, and other hardware to communicate directly with Windows. However, a faulty or incompatible driver can wreck the entire system. For example, if an older driver conflicts with changes in Windows 11, the failure can cause a system crash or a BSOD.

An in-place upgrade is also very different from installing Windows 11 on a clean system. When you choose to keep your files, applications, and settings, Windows preserves much of the existing software environment, including drivers, configuration files, background services, and software components that may have accumulated over several years. Most of these will continue working without problems, but outdated components can create conflicts after the upgrade.

Microsoft isn't solely responsible for every driver running on your PC. Hardware manufacturers and OEMs develop and maintain drivers for components like graphics cards, motherboards, audio hardware, network adapters, and more. And sometimes, they don't do a very good job of maintaining these drivers.

Windows 10 is almost dead, but this tool can help your old PC upgrade to Windows 11

Your PC still has life left in it

22
By  João Carrasqueira

A Windows 11 installation can fix most of the issues

Always do a fresh install

A clean Windows 11 installation fixes many of these crashes. When you boot from a USB drive, erase the system partition, and reinstall Windows, the process removes old driver packages, configuration files, services, and applications.

Windows 11 then starts with the drivers included with the operating system. Once the PC connects to the internet, Windows Update automatically downloads drivers for the detected hardware. You can then install the latest chipset, graphics, audio, and network drivers from the PC or component manufacturer.

With the earliest versions of Windows, a clean installation was the only way to move from one version to another. In-place upgrades arrived with Windows 95 and made the process much easier. Even so, IT professionals and Windows power users have continued recommending clean installs for decades.

The benefits extend beyond drivers. For one, a clean installation avoids preloaded software, often called “bloatware.” OEM PCs commonly include trialware, vendor utilities, and unwanted applications in their factory Windows images. A clean installation using Microsoft’s installation media skips all of that, including the pop-ups, nag screens, and other annoyances.

A clean Windows 11 installation also brings your PC’s security up to date. Windows continues to gain new security features and capabilities over time, including between Windows 11 releases and, more substantially, between Windows 10 and Windows 11. Some of these features can only be enabled during a clean installation. A clean install also removes older configurations that can prevent other security features from working properly.

You can always manually update your drivers

If you simply don't have enough time to do a fresh install

A clean installation isn't always practical for everyone, especially if you upgraded to Windows 10 or Windows 11 a long time ago and have been using the same installation ever since. I upgraded from Windows 10 to Windows 11 because I simply didn't have time for a fresh install. It's been four years since I upgraded, and I've been manually updating drivers whenever I run into an issue or remember I haven't updated one in a while.

If you're also planning to continue without a fresh installation, you can address issues, crashes, and BSODs by gradually replacing old drivers with versions made for Windows 11. You would want to start with graphics, chipset, storage, network, and audio drivers, since these components interact closely with the operating system.

The important part is to check that each download lists Windows 11 as a supported operating system. Don't assume a driver is compatible because it worked under Windows 10 or survived the upgrade. You should also check Settings -> Windows Update -> Advanced options -> Optional updates, since Windows sometimes places driver updates there instead of installing them automatically.

Windows 11 gets more hate than it deserves

Windows 11 gets more hate than it deserves, especially when every crash, slowdown, or BSOD is immediately blamed on the operating system itself. Microsoft has certainly made questionable interface and usability decisions, but that does not automatically make Windows 11 unstable.

It's just not worth the hassle anymore.
